newsitem.title: USA: Fla. case statistician praises EPA smoke report.
newsitem.headline: Fla. case statistician praises EPA smoke report.

text.p: Attorneys pressing a landmark flight attendants' lawsuit against the tobacco industry Thursday called as a witness a statistician who praised a 1993 Environmental Protection Agency report on secondhand smoking as an outstanding numerical analysis.

"I quickly recognised that it was one of the best examples I had ever seen of a careful, scientifically correct use of numbers in a public health question," said Fred Bookstein, a University of Michigan research scientist.
In the report, the EPA concluded secondhand smoke is a "Class A" carcinogen, causes lung cancer and is responsible for about 3,000 lung cancer deaths among nonsmokers each year.

The report said 24 of 30 studies had found a higher incidence of lung cancer in nonsmoking wives of smokers than in nonsmokers married to nonsmokers, a frequency that had only a one in 1,000 chance of occurring.
"The conclusions that have been reached by the EPA are perfectly properly drawn, from my professional point of view," he said.
In contrast, Bookstein dismissed tobacco challenges to the data. "I found them to be without merit," he said.

Bookstein was called as a witness for plaintiffs in Norma Broin et al vs. Philip Morris Cos. Inc. et al, a $5 billion class-action lawsuit brought against the tobacco industry on behalf of thousands of flight attendants who claim they were sickened by breathing secondhand cigarette smoke on U.S.-based aircraft.
Now in its third week of testimony, the Dade County Circuit Court case is the first class action and first secondhand smoke lawsuit against major cigarette companies to make it to trial.

Earlier Thursday, the jury watched the end of a videotaped deposition of Dr. Freddy Homburger, a pathologist who performed years of research funded by the Council for Tobacco Research. On Wednesday, Homburger testified on videotape that the industry pressured him not to publicise data showing that hamsters developed cancer after inhaling tobacco smoke.

In the case, the plaintiffs' attorneys, Stanley and Susan Rosenblatt, want to convince the jury not only that secondhand smoke made the flight attendants sick but also that the tobacco industry committed fraud by trying to deceive the public about the risks of smoking.
During the videotaped cross-examination, tobacco attorneys said Homburger had had many chances to publish and asked why he remembered some events in the early 1970s, but not others.
Homburger, 81, answered that his spotty memory was logical. He asked, "Don't you remember when you get hurt in the face ... or when someone calls you a bad name?"

Homburger was also a witness in a case brought against tobacco on behalf of Rose Cipollone, a smoker who died of lung cancer. In that case, the first tobacco lawsuit reviewed by the Supreme Court, a jury in 1988 awarded the family $400,000. The award was overturned on appeal and the case eventually dropped.

The plaintiffs are expected to present witnesses for about two more weeks. After the plaintiffs rest, attorneys for the tobacco defendants -- Philip Morris Inc., Philip Morris Products Inc., R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., Lorillard Inc., Lorillard Tobacco Co., Brooke Group Ltd., Liggett Group Inc., Brown & Williamson Tobacco Co., the Tobacco Institute and the Council for Tobacco Research -- will present their case.
